transcript:
Meeting header: 
Date: 2026-10-17 15:00 PT | Duration: 58m | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (SE), Sara (CSM); Priya (Arbor Head ML), Tom (VP Eng), Dana (SRE), Michael (PM)

[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick agenda — run through the anomalous spike you saw last week, walk through cost and latency impact, discuss short vs mid-term choices (hosted burst, dedicated pools, private), and align on next steps for the pilot and compliance review.
[00:18] Priya (Arbor): Thanks Maya. Yeah we appreciate it. We got a really surprising jump last Tuesday, like 3x baseline for a two hour window. It spiked costs and our frontend started hitting tail latency.
[00:31] Tom (Customer): Right, core question — was it caused by our indexing job accidentally hitting inference endpoints, or is it a traffic pattern issue? We want to prevent billing surprises.
[00:42] Liam (Redwood SE): Got it. From the telemetry you shared, we already saw a high token-per-request increase in that window. There were also many small concurrent chat sessions which increased context length. Could be a mix.
[00:55] Dana (SRE): One data point — our job scheduler reported a retry storm at 10:12 which coincides with the start of the spike. I can share logs.
[01:05] Maya: Perfect. That's consistent with what the billing trace shows. Two common mitigation patterns: prefix/KV caching for repeated contexts, and routing heavy background jobs to a separate capacity tier or dedicated pool.
[01:20] Michael (PM): Can you level-set us on cost delta for a dedicated pool vs using hosted with burst caps? We need numbers for exec.
[01:28] Sara (CSM): We'll provide modeled examples — quick rule of thumb: dedicated tends to lower unit cost at sustained throughput but has reservation/commitment. Hosted is flexible but you pay for peak unless caching/batching reduces tokens.
[01:45] Priya: We also need to know SLA differences — our users care about 99th percentile latency. If hosted has variance that's a problem.
[01:55] Liam: On that, Dedicated allows you to pin hardware and we can configure autoscale policies with headroom — that gives more consistent p99. For hosted, we have smart routing and fallback but under global peaks you might see tail latency spikes.
[02:12] Tom: Ok, show us an example configuration. What's the minimum reserve we'd need to cover the observed 3x two-hour spike?
[02:21] Liam: Based on your peak qps and average tokens, to get <400ms p95 you'd need approx 6 reserved GPUs of the X1 class for that window. If that's only occasional, cost may not justify reserve. Alternative: burst capacity plus pre-warming and an isolation route for long-running batch jobs.
[02:40] Priya: What about quantization / model selection? We currently run a 70B open model for most inference. Can switching to a cheaper quantized variant help during spikes?
[02:50] Liam: Absolutely. For conversational flows with bounded fidelity, a quantized 70B-lite or a 30B variant reduces token cost and latency. Redwood Optimize can recommend model profiles per route. We'll include a profile later.
[03:04] Dana: Back to the spike root cause — once I pull the scheduler logs and show the timing, is Redwood able to stitch traces to see which client keys caused the largest token burn?
[03:15] Maya: Yes, with the request-level traces you gave us we can correlate API keys and seen prompts. We usually don't expose raw customer data, we do sanitized attribution — but for debugging you can provide a masked key mapping and we can point to request-hash ranges.
[03:30] Priya: Ok we'll prepare that.
[03:34] [04:00] — brief cross talk as people share links
[04:05] Tom: Another ask — our security/compliance team needs network diagrams and KMS/HSM details. They asked if Redwood Private (VPC) is available for our PHI-laden flows.
[04:18] Maya: Yes. Redwood Private supports customer-managed VPC peering and can be deployed on-prem for air-gapped needs. For cloud VPC we integrate with customer KMS, and we provide audit logs and key rotation guidance. I can put the SOC2/ISO packet and network diagram in the shared folder.
[04:33] Michael: Any differences in feature parity between Hosted and Private?
[04:38] Liam: Feature parity is close; the biggest gaps historically are third-party telemetry integrations and some managed autoscale behaviors. For Private we recommend a slightly different autoscaler setup and we can provide runbooks. We'll list differences in the SOW.
[04:53] Priya: Great. For the pilot we want to test both cost and reliability — can we design a two-week split where first week is hosted with optimizations, second is dedicated pool to compare?
[05:04] Maya: That's a good plan. We usually do a phased pilot: smoke tests, 24–72hr continuous benchmark, then a production-like ramp. For your ask we can do Hosted w/ caching + quantized model for the week, then dedicated reserved capacity the next week and compare metrics.
[05:21] Dana: Can we also get a stress test that simulates our peak plus background job interference?
[05:26] Liam: Yes we'll build a synthetic runner that replays real session distributions — need your consent on request shapes.
[05:33] Priya: On the cost side, are there ways we can avoid per-token surprises? For example, cap billable tokens per key or alerts?
[05:42] Sara: There are quota and alerting features; you can set per-key quotas and throttles, and we can configure early-fail policies for non-critical flows. We'll also enable token burn alerts to the devops Slack channel.
[05:56] Tom: Competitor question — we evaluated VendorX and Anthropic earlier; how does Redwood's fallback & multi-variant routing compare?
[06:05] Liam: We support automated model routing by policy: latency-first, cost-first, or region-first. On fallback, Redwood can transparently fail over to a cheaper variant or different region; we keep consistent session context with KV cache where possible. That reduces perceived errors during congestion compared to simple endpoint failover.
[06:23] Priya: Nice. For the executive summary we'll need clear cost delta tables. Can you send a modeled spreadsheet showing our current monthly baseline, cost with 2hr spike x3, and two pilot configurations?
[06:34] Maya: Yes — action item on me. We'll model baseline, hosted-optimized, and dedicated-reserve math with assumptions called out.
[06:43] [06:50] Liam: Quick note on metrics we'll capture during benchmark: p50/p95/p99 latency, token/sec, error-rate, tail-kv cache hit rate, and cost-per-1M tokens. Also memory pressure and TPU/GPU saturation graphs.
[07:02] Dana: Will you share traces in Prometheus/Grafana-friendly exports?
[07:06] Liam: We can provide CSV/JSON and a Grafana dashboard export; for Private we can ship a dashboard pack you can import.
[07:14] Michael: About rollback and canary — how do we test model changes without affecting production?
[07:19] Maya: Redwood supports canary routing and automatic fallback policies. We can route a percentage of traffic to a new model variant or quantized profile and roll back if metrics worsen. We'll propose a canary ramp in the SOW.
[07:33] Priya: What about monitoring for hallucination/regression? We need quality guards, not just perf.
[07:39] Liam: Redwood Optimize can track evals against a prompt set and flag quality regressions tied to prompts. We'll attach a lightweight eval harness for your test prompts.
[07:52] Tom: On data retention — our legal team wants to ensure ephemeral traces aren't stored beyond X days. What's Redwood's retention policy and can it be overridden per customer?
[08:02] Sara: Hosted has standard retention windows; for Private you can set retention and we support event-level purging on request. We'll include retention options in the security packet.
[08:12] Priya: For the spike forensic — timeline? How fast can Redwood produce a sanitized attribution to help our incident post-mortem?
[08:20] Maya: With the logs you sent we can deliver an initial attribution within 48 hours and a full forensic report within five business days, assuming you provide masked key mapping.
[08:31] [08:45] Tom: Sounds reasonable.
[08:47] Michael: There was a comment earlier about caching — are we talking about prefix caching, KV caching, or both?
[08:54] Liam: Both; prefix caching helps identical inputs, KV cache preserves model cached context across sessions for multi-turn chats. The latter reduces compute for repeated long histories. We'll propose which routes to enable KV cache for.
[09:07] Dana: Any change on our side to integrate KV cache?
[09:10] Liam: Minimal: handle session identifiers and ensure secrets aren't included in the context. We have client-side SDK guidance.
[09:18] Priya: For the pilot metrics, is it possible to measure cost attribution by feature (search, chat, summarization)?
[09:24] Sara: Yes, we can add route-level cost attribution and tag tokens by feature; you'll get a breakdown per route.
[09:31] [09:45] — short silence as documents are shared
[09:48] Tom: A security nuance — SSO and RBAC for admin portals. Can we sync SAML/SCIM for our team?
[09:56] Maya: Yes, Redwood supports SAML SSO and SCIM for user provisioning. We'll send the metadata and steps.
[10:05] Priya: On timeline — if we start the pilot 10/25, what do you need from us before then?
[10:11] Maya: Deliverables: signed pilot SOW, masked key mapping for forensic, peak-window definition, list of test prompts for quality evals, and compliance reviewer contact. If we get those by 10/20 we can stand up pilot infra by 10/25.
[10:23] Dana: Ok we'll aim for that.
[10:26] Liam: Quick technical note — for the benchmark we'll spin up a dedicated cluster that mirrors your proposed dedicated config and run a few synthetic phases: steady-state, ramp, and stress with random retries to measure grace under burst. We'll capture GPU metrics and token churn.
[10:43] Michael: When we compare results, will you provide cost normalized to our committed currency?
[10:47] Sara: Yes we'll present cost per 1M tokens normalized to your current price tier and projected committed rates.
[10:55] Priya: One more exec question — if we commit to dedicated capacity, what is the minimum contract and typical SLAs?
[11:02] Maya: Typical reserved contracts start at 3 months with monthly or annual billing options. SLA depends on tier; we'll include an SLA appendix with uptime and latency targets at each tier in the SOW.
[11:14] Tom: Any manual operational overhead for us during the dedicated phase?
[11:18] Liam: For Redwood Dedicated we handle most infra ops; you'll need to coordinate autoscale policy changes and capacity increase requests with our infra team for large forecast changes. We also recommend a runbook walkthrough.
[11:31] [11:45] Priya: Let's talk about the exact metrics we want in the QBR table — can you propose a template?
[11:50] Sara: We'll propose a one-page dashboard: baseline usage, anomalies (count/duration), cost delta, p50/p95/p99, error rate, model quality score, and recommended action. We'll attach an appendix with raw CSVs.
[12:06] Michael: On the pilot SOW — will you include rollback/rescue steps if performance regresses mid-pilot?
[12:12] Maya: Yes standard SOW includes rollback policy and escalation path.
[12:18] Tom: One last risk — what if the spike is malicious or a crawler? Will Redwood help with rate-limiting and automated blocking?
[12:27] Liam: We can enable per-key rate limits and detect anomalous patterns; for aggressive cases we can implement temporary throttles and provide an audit trail.
[12:36] Priya: Ok great. Do you have any notes on long-term cost governance? We want to avoid surprises as we scale.
[12:43] Sara: We recommend guardrails: per-route quota, scheduled scaling windows, model-tier routing policies, and monthly usage reviews. Redwood Optimize can give ongoing recommendations.
[12:57] [13:05] Maya: All right let's recap and assign owners. Action items are in the meeting notes. We propose the capacity workshop on 2026-10-24 at 10am PT — does that work for Arbor team?
[13:17] Dana: Works for me.
[13:19] Priya: Works.
[13:21] Tom: Fine.
[13:23] Maya: Great. I'll email the pilot SOW draft and pricing spreadsheet today, Liam will start the benchmarking plan, and Sara will post the notes to CRM.
[13:31] Michael: Thanks everyone.
[13:33] [13:40] — informal wrap-up and people drop off

Notes on transcript artifacts: some speaker labels were noisy in automated transcription (e.g., "Liam O'Neil" instead of O'Neill; vendor name VendorX was transcribed as 'Vendor Ex' in parts). A sanitized log, CSVs, and security packet will be attached to CRM entry.

End of transcript.
